entries.title: Agrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient Rome
entries.summary: This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for powerIf you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week, Robert Harris has you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assas
entries.content:
If you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week, Robert Harris has you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assassination of Julius Caesar, with all the bickering and bloodshed that follows, on to the decisive battle of Actium and Octavius’s apotheosis as Caesar Augustus. We meet Cicero, Fulvia, Lepidus, two Caesars and a burly Antony (“Imagine, if you will, a statue of Hercules with a club in one hand, a wineskin in the other”).

Here’s the clever bit: he narrates it all from the point of view of Octavius’s right-hand man, Agrippa, a much less well-remembered figure. Harris tells us he “left behind no speeches, few letters and only a couple of sentences of direct quotation”. Yet Agrippa was “effective co-ruler of the Roman world for many years” and “the greatest general of the period”. Octavius couldn’t have risen without him, but he seems to have done his best to write him out of the story afterwards, according him only two passing mentions in the Res Gestae Divi Augusti.

Harris’s Octavius is vain, clever, sickly, ambitious, manipulative and prickly. His childhood friend Agrippa, the only person he sort-of trusts, is established early on as a bit of a meathead. Their first encounter is when Agrippa duffs up a couple of bullies he catches picking on a weaker boy; mostly for the pleasure of duffing a couple of people up. He doesn’t know at the time that the beneficiary of this duffing is Caesar’s nephew. They become friends: “He helped me with my classwork. I showed him how to fight.” They share a teacher: “He instilled in Octavius especially a lifelong love of poetry, although my literary tastes, to his despair, have always tended towards works on engineering and military history.” Even as they rise to power, our man’s eye is on the duffing. Octavius returns to Rome amid great danger to give a rousing speech, and Agrippa reports only: “His voice carried well. I did not pay much attention to what he said. I was too preoccupied scanning his audience for potential assassins.”

Harris’s framing conceit is that the text we are reading is Agrippa’s memoir, written in some haste and high feeling. Agrippa, now an old man of 50, has come home early from an expedition to duff up the barbarians in Illyricum. He has a gammy leg, which is about to kill him. He limps in to find his wife in bed with his son-in-law. Since the son-in-law is also the emperor’s adopted son, he hesitates to get busy with his sword and instead retreats to his chamber. He’s feeling a bit sorry for himself and, uncharacteristically, he turns to words.

It is a sign of Harris’s discipline as a novelist that he has Agrippa tell his tale in almost comically unambitious prose. There’s a lot of pipe-laying in the military history department, of the “then the legions would wheel around the far side of the Black Sea by way of Hyrcania, the Captain Sea and the Caucasus, and march west” type. And he’s a bastard for an aqueduct, is Agrippa. Loves them; maybe even more than having a scrap. He’s never happier than when building infrastructure and explaining the engineering principles and logistics to the reader.

When Agrippa is stirred to reflection, he tends to reach for a well-worn phrase. “The sickly, pungent stink of death lurked round every corner.” “Mercy was now the order of the day.” “War, which I had once so relished, was gouged into the countryside like an open wound.” “Power makes monsters of us all.” “In the words of the old saying – if you strike at the king, you must be sure not to miss.” (That particular old saying, I think, comes from The Wire, but never mind.)

But from all this elegantly drab stuff emerges a more subtle portrait of the man and the age than you might expect. You get a persuasive portrait of a Rome exhausted by civil strife, and of the serpentine manoeuvrings of its rulers. Everyone is betraying everyone else, raising armies, marrying each other’s children, forming and breaking alliances. It’s hectic. And, gosh, all these people redrawing the map of the world and changing the course of history are young. The plot twist – a feature of scholarly speculation since 1937, Harris’s afterword tells us – concerns the real parentage of the apparently low-born Agrippa.

But that, like much else, it suited him to keep quiet about. His most enduring real-world monument is seven terse words in stone above the entrance to the Pantheon: M F AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIUM FECIT. “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, in his third consulship, did it.”

entries.title: The Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatments
entries.summary: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted himWhich, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you d
entries.content:
Which, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you don’t have to choose between them. He’s all five wrapped into one objectionable package, and so much more besides.

The tale begins with the Sonoran desert toad, an improbable amphibian that spends most of its life hiding underground in the baking badlands along the Mexico-Arizona border, and has done so blamelessly for millions of years. Whenever it rains, the toads emerge from their hiding places to mate, laying strings of eggs wherever water has pooled.

There have long been fanciful tales of hippies getting high by licking toads, but these ones are the real deal: the world’s only known psychoactive animal. In the early 1980s, humans discovered that the toad’s poison glands secrete a venom that contains, among other chemicals, 5-MeO-DMT, a potent hallucinogen also known as the “God molecule”. The first known user squirted the glands of a toad that his dog caught on to the windscreen of his Chevy Sport, where the substance dried and he smoked it.

He wrote a manual describing “an overload of thoughts and perception, brief collapse of the ego, and loss of the space-time continuum”. It was, in short, a lot. The prospect enticed other users, and those included, two decades later, Rettig.

A troubled young man from Mexico, Rettig started smoking dried toad venom in the first decade of this century, and claims it helped him kick his crack cocaine habit. That was a time when popular interest in psychedelics was re-emerging after the long post-1960s winter, and many medical practitioners were wondering if these mind-altering chemicals couldn’t help patients who weren’t responding to their traditional treatments. Much of the focus had been on LSD, psilocybin and ketamine, but 5-MeO-DMT provided a whole new level of experience. The shatteringly powerful effect of the chemical was said to replicate the effect of years of therapy in just half an hour, which is clearly an attractive prospect for a psychedelic entrepreneur keen to maximise patient throughput.

Rettig was no pioneer in his enthusiasm for smoking toad. Instead, his contribution was to create a tradition for this new hallucinogen, thus giving it the kind of mystical authenticity that peyote, morning glory and ayahuasca gain among devotees thanks to their association with ancient Native American rituals.

The Seri people, who live between the Sonoran Desert and the Gulf of California, have suffered terribly both under the Spanish colony of Mexico, and the independent republic. By the time Rettig visited in 2011, there were just a few hundred of them left, living in squalid and trash-strewn villages, predated upon by drug cartels and plagued by addiction. Rettig adopted their chants, claimed their ancient toad-based tradition had been suppressed and was only now being rediscovered, and started presenting himself globally as a practitioner of indigenous medicine.

There may well be a medical case for treatment with 5-MeO-DMT, but it’s hard to see any argument for treating people with it the way that Rettig did. He offered huge doses with minimal screening, sometimes inflicting treatment forcibly. (In response to footage of him being aggressive to clients, he told De Greef: “I am open to acknowledge that some of my actions might be disturbing for most audiences, but this is a very deep therapeutic work.”) He engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakes. Rettig claims: “My work has been misunderstood, misinterpreted, and misused.” But it is an incredibly dark tale.

A different writer might have been tempted to go gonzo, to smoke toad himself, and to come back with stories of ego death, the space-time continuum and the rest of it, but Kimon de Greef mercifully avoids that temptation. A South African, he came to the story of Rettig not from the world of psychedelics but from researching wildlife smuggling, which gives him an unusually clear-eyed view of how grim these kinds of practices are.

A lot of the reporting for this book began life in the New Yorker, and it is as methodical, exacting, well-written and exceptionally reported as you’d expect. Fortunately, De Greef avoids the fate that can befall books based on American magazine articles that fail to break free of them, and really enjoys the extra space. He launches into entertaining digressions into how exactly the toads’ psychedelic powers were first discovered, into how pharmaceutical companies are harnessing 5-MeO-DMT for their own ends, introducing fascinating cameos, before he returns to the main story.

He is not a man for grand conclusions, but I challenge any reader not to see this highly enjoyable book as a parable for so much that’s wrong with the current economy. Everything from the undeserved authority of charlatans, to the rampant exploitation of the natural world, to the hiding of hyper-capitalism behind a shield of cod-mystical woo-woo: it’s all in there.

Rettig’s ultimate fate has been to be largely forgotten by the movement he helped to popularise, which has mutated and expanded at the speed of social media, with new influencers appearing and new markets opening. The toads, meanwhile, have become just another commodity to be exploited.

entries.title: ‘It is not only a future certainty – the disaster is already here’: why we need climate fiction
entries.summary: As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisisEarlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. Everywhere I went, the heat broke records. In Italy, Germany and Spain, I sought refuge from the afternoon sun in air-conditioned hotels. In normally
entries.content:
Earlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. Everywhere I went, the heat broke records. In Italy, Germany and Spain, I sought refuge from the afternoon sun in air-conditioned hotels. In normally temperate Zurich, it averaged 37 degrees. I jumped into the Limmat for relief. On my final day in Warsaw, Poland had never been hotter – one of 14 countries to hit a historic high. In June, when I left to return to the US, Europe was scorching. At the end of July, as I write this, it is burning.

Since the heatwaves began, there have been more than 10,000 excess deaths. Yet for many, myself included, the high temperatures brought nothing more than inconvenience – uncomfortable commutes, heat rash, less time outdoors. This seems to be a defining feature of today’s climate crisis; deadly for some, banal for others. Even when the world is on fire, it somehow doesn’t feel like an emergency for everyone.

This disparity cast my mind back to Hurricane Sandy in 2012. I was living in New York, one of millions ordered to shelter in place. (I was lucky – hundreds of thousands were ordered to evacuate their homes.) I followed instructions. I stayed in my warm, dry apartment on the Upper West Side, watching trees swaying violently against the dark sky. The next morning, the rain had stopped; the sun was out, the air was still again and the power was still on. When I went outside to survey the damage, there was little to see except a few broken branches. The mood in my neighbourhood was jovial. The subways were closed, schools were shut, work was called off. Brunch was on.

In other parts of the city, it was a different story. Whole fleets of taxi cabs submerged in water, their canary yellow roofs peeking out; a huge midtown crane snapped cleanly in half; the collapsed wall of an apartment building. I watched and rewatched a video of a power plant exploding. Half a million people, including most of the residents of lower Manhattan, were now without electricity. The American news outlets focused almost exclusively on New York. The international news sites told a more complete story: Sandy killed 233 people in eight countries and caused $70bn in damage.

Several days after the storm, I volunteered in Chinatown, distributing basic goods – batteries, canned food and bottled water – to elderly people who lived on the highest floors of public housing buildings and hadn’t yet ventured outside since the storm. (the lifts weren’t working and they weren’t able to take the stairs). The apartments smelled of rotting food and unflushed toilets. The national guard rolled through the streets in tanks; rats brazenly stalked the pavements and Red Cross workers posed for photographs with locals. Research labs at NYU lost their lab animals during the storm; the news reported them dead, but rumours spread that the rodent population of the city had grown by 10,000 transgenic mice and rats.

New rules governed downtown life. Bars served free drinks by candlelight, neighbourhood people with handmade signs offered water to passersby, small shops offered free charging stations. The roads around Ground Zero stayed flooded for weeks; the water was green and brackish. Amid the darkness, one building stayed lit, its squares of gold stretched into the sky. Goldman Sachs would not be stopped.

In the days and weeks after Sandy, I was struck by many disparities: between downtown darkness and uptown light; between those who were able to escape the city to second homes and those who had nowhere else to go; between the countries with a quick, organised disaster response and those that relied entirely on community help. I also found myself thinking about the natural disasters I had heard about as a child and teenager growing up in Singapore: the 1999 Odisha cyclone, the 2003 heatwave across India, the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, the 2006 Southern Leyte mudslide in the Philippines, the 2007 cyclone in Bangladesh. These were disasters with much higher death tolls that I realised many people had never heard about.

When Sandy made landfall in 2012, I had just begun my PhD in English literature. For work, I read canonical 19th-century realist novels; for pleasure, I read contemporary literary fiction. I searched for novels about the environment but often found myself disappointed. In many, the severe consequences of the climate crisis were packaged as a future possibility – something to come, one day. But the climate crisis is not only a future certainty, it is past and present truth. The disaster is already here.

Several years after Sandy, I read Amitav Ghosh’s The Great Derangement, in which he argues that literary fiction has failed us. Ghosh perfectly articulated my disappointment about the climate fiction, or cli-fi, I had read. But he went further. Ghosh listed the reasons the modern novel was unsuited to the challenge of representing the climate crisis. One, contemporary western novels had become “ever more radically centred on the individual psyche”. Two, unlike other genres, novels can’t range freely over space and time. Three, our literary imagination had become “radically centred on the human”. And four, the climate crisis is defined by improbable events and “probability and the modern novels are twins”.

When I first read The Great Derangement, I agreed with Ghosh that “the climate crisis is also a crisis of culture, and thus of the imagination”. But I also wondered whether it would be possible to write what he said didn’t exist but should: serious literary fiction that captures both the freak event and the mundane truth of the climate crisis.

Ghosh laid down a gauntlet; I thought I’d try to pick it up. Over the next eight years, I wrote a novel that moves towards two cataclysmic events – Hurricane Sandy and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami – but also documents the slow violence that unfolds in both New York and Thailand. My debut novel, Under Water, seeks to represent climate change in the very form Ghosh suggests is ill-suited to the task: a realist novel centred on a single individual.

It is true, as Ghosh notes, that, unlike epics, novels do not usually bring multiple universes into conjunction. But a realist novel centred on a bourgeois subject in today’s globalised world can in fact move across space and time. A single individual might, as my protagonist Marissa does, grow up on a barely inhabited island in south-east Asia and then, a decade later, live as an adult in a large metropolis on the east coast of the United States.

My book also responds to Ghosh’s striking claim that the modern novel was “never forced to confront the centrality of the improbable”. In Under Water, I try to imbue Hurricane Sandy, a highly improbable event, with expectation. Because of her childhood and her past, Marissa experiences the approach of Sandy differently from other inhabitants of the city.

Under Water is a riposte to Ghosh’s claim that the contemporary realist novel is destined to fail us. A single novel cannot show everything, everywhere, all at once. But it can, more effectively than any other cultural form, wield what I think is still one of our best weapons against this or any other crisis: the determination to pay close, careful attention to the people and places we are losing, every day.

entries.title: Art Spiegelman: ‘The US needs a counter-revolution’
entries.summary: More than four decades after his Holocaust story Maus transformed the graphic novel genre, Art Spiegelman discusses Trump, the shadow of 9/11 and the rise of fascism in AmericaWhen the cartoonist Art Spiegelman began dating his future wife, Françoise Mouly, in the mid 70s, she would tell him not to worry about walking her home, because even the New York muggers didn’t bother venturing to where she
entries.content:
When the cartoonist Art Spiegelman began dating his future wife, Françoise Mouly, in the mid 70s, she would tell him not to worry about walking her home, because even the New York muggers didn’t bother venturing to where she lived in Soho. He moved in with her quite suddenly not long after, when his apartment in Greenwich Village burned down. His landlord, who lived on the ground floor, was a hoarder – once, when he came to collect Spiegelman’s rent, a cockroach crawled up from under his shirt collar – and eventually his accumulated junk caught alight.

This feels like a quintessential New York story, but then much of Spiegelman’s life does, or at least fits with the kind of stories we like to tell ourselves about the city. The Soho apartment Spiegelman and Mouly have lived in for five decades is worth millions now and is surrounded by high-end designers; his studio, down the road, is above a branch of Tiffany’s. “It’s just kind of an embarrassment, I mean Tiffany’s is not my class,” says Spiegelman, who refers to these flash new arrivals, dismissively, as “very fancy airport mall stores”.

The couple used to print their own “oddball” comics from a printing press that Mouly, who had dropped out of architecture school in France, installed in their house. Today, they are a New York art establishment power couple. Mouly is the art editor of the New Yorker, having been recruited by Tina Brown in the 90s, when she was looking to make the highbrow magazine “hot”. Spiegelman, who in 1992 became the first cartoonist to win a Pulitzer prize for Maus, a graphic novel about his father’s memories of the Holocaust, has done more than anyone to establish comics as a serious art form, capable of tackling difficult political and personal subjects. The couple’s trajectory had “its own weird logic, although it wouldn’t be anyone else’s. It’s not a ‘recipe for success’,” Spiegelman jokes. “We were wilfully just doing what we wanted to do.”

He is 78 years old, slight and scruffy-looking, with a grizzled goatee and wispy grey hair, and he can still talk faster than most people can think. He offers me a coffee when I arrive at his home on a sweltering June day, but then keeps getting distracted from making it by his own anecdotes. He takes me on an impromptu tour, showing me the living room that held Mouly’s huge, 1,000lb Multilith printing press, until they had a toddler and it became too dangerous to keep. There is a mural painted by the cartoonist Gary Panter on the living room wall, and another just above their bed, painted to replace a set of bookshelves that collapsed onto the couple when they were asleep, breaking Mouly’s nose and prompting a big book clear out. “Is this book worth dying for?” Spiegelman says they asked of themselves, a more hardcore alternative to Swedish death cleaning, but even so there are full bookshelves in every room, and pieces of art and curios everywhere.

As a young man, Spiegelman earned a living designing collectible parody cards for Topps bubblegum, while cutting his teeth in San Francisco’s underground comics scene. After moving to New York, he started Raw magazine with Mouly. Raw published experimental work by comic artists from all over the world, and “it created its own Potemkin village of, yes, all these artists have one thing in common, which is they ain’t like each other,” he recalls. Maus was initially serialised as an insert in Raw – new issues came out sporadically, whenever Spiegelman had finished a chapter.

He struggled to find a publisher for the book, because no one knew what to do with such an unusual work, an autobiographical history of the Holocaust that depicted Jews as mice and Nazis as cats. The responses were “pretty universal that whatever this is, is interesting. But it’s not publishable,” he says. Eventually, Pantheon published it, and Maus became a bestseller. Spiegelman has said he struggled to emerge from the shadow of his best-known creation, but when I ask if he still feels ambivalent about Maus’s success he replies, “I’m ambivalent about absolutely everything … I knew that I wanted it to be read, but it just didn’t occur to me that it would become a phenomenon, it was such an outlier.”

Maus took 13 years to make. For Spiegelman, making comics is often a tortuous process. If many artists complain of creative blocks, then what he experiences is more like a “blockade: there’s no way in or out. I think it’s like a version of impostor syndrome,” he says. “I know I’ve done comics before and they work, but I have no idea how to do it when I start a new one … I have to rethink what it might be to make a comic.” He feels acutely aware of his limitations – “I always understood that I wasn’t the best drawer on the block” – and every square must be painstakingly reworked, dozens of times. “It seems like I don’t function well. I mean, I don’t go: ‘OK, I finished this graphic novel, I’ll do another one – by God!’ – and then off to the races. Something has to make me go through what is such a difficult process for me,” he says.

Spiegelman had virtually stopped making comics and was focused on writing essays and designing covers for the New Yorker when the 9/11 attacks took place. The ground shook, and from his Soho apartment he could see the north tower burning. His first thought was to run to collect his daughter Nadja, who had just started high school at the foot of the towers. Then, fearing that the United Nations might be targeted next, they rushed uptown to collect his son Dash, who was at the UN School. This was the kind of catastrophe his parents, both Auschwitz survivors, had always warned him about, when world history and personal history collide. “I’m not going to get past this unless I start drawing about it,” he realised afterwards, and he vowed to make comics again.

He produced a series about 9/11 for the German magazine Die Zeit, which was later run by other European magazines and American Jewish weekly the Forward. On one page he describes himself as “equally terrorised by al-Qaida and by my own government”. He felt that other American publications were too quiescent in the aftermath of the attacks, and not yet receptive to his fear that the US government was using 9/11 as cover for a massive crackdown on civil liberties and to launch xenophobic wars. “Sigh! It’s hard to be an artist who is consistently Seconds Ahead of His Time,” he writes in the foreword to In the Shadow of No Towers, a book that compiled these comics and is being reissued to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. (Although, he says, it may come out late – a shipment has been held up in the strait of Hormuz.)

Why was he so alert to the implications for US civil liberties? “Well, my tendency is not to trust the government, so that came easily,” he says. “But it also seems so obvious, like all of a sudden there were police cars and military trucks on Canal Street. We were being told where we could walk, where we couldn’t walk, what we could say, what we couldn’t say. It’s visceral. It’s not like: ‘OK, I’ve read this book on propaganda and here’s how it works.’” Spiegelman notes the direct link between the post-9/11 security crackdowns and some of the excesses of the Trump administration: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Ice, was created in the aftermath of the terror attacks.

A theme running through Spiegelman’s work is trauma, and its long and toxic aftermath. His parents were Polish Jews who survived the camps but lost most of their family, including their first-born son, Richieu, during the Holocaust. They resettled in Rego Park, Queens, where Spiegelman was born in 1948. In 1968, his mother, Anja, killed herself. Spiegelman was living with his parents at the time, having been hospitalised after suffering a psychotic episode while studying at Harpur College, New York, where he had been experimenting with every drug he could find. Maus is partly about Spiegelman’s fraught relationship with his father Vladek, who is depicted as mean, difficult and racist – a man who complicates the comforting lie we tell ourselves that suffering must make a person kinder or nobler. In one comic, published in Breakdowns (2008), Spiegelman hands a treasure chest to his young son, a family heirloom that was given to him by his own father. Excited, Dash opens the box, only to reveal a terrifying monster. “It’s magical! It makes you feel so worthless you don’t believe you even have the right to breathe,” Spiegelman tells his son, a cigarette hanging from his mouth.

When it comes to 9/11, however, Spiegelman’s perspective has shifted. He no longer views the day as an “end of the world moment”. “It was a big deal. But it was a small big deal compared to the big deals that are going on now,” he tells me. “I’d much rather be in New York than in Iran, for example.”

Around 50 minutes after Spiegelman fires up his Nespresso machine, he finishes making two coffees, and we carry them up to his sunny roof terrace, which as he promised has beautiful views of downtown Manhattan. Spiegelman muses that the US’s volatile politics might reflect humankind’s natural tendency to self-destruction. “I guess, after a while, you get restless, so if you get too comfortable you create problems for yourself, even in more mundane, small-time life, never mind as a nation. At this point, we just had the bad luck of having a megalomaniac walking onto the scene,” he says, of the Trump presidency. American politics is, after all, “entertaining if you don’t give a shit, if you’re nihilistic”.

Spiegelman’s mood is sombre as he discusses how Trump has “very effectively dismantled” the country’s democratic ideals: “Whatever the ideals were, we never lived up to them, but at least we had them. Now it’s all so cynical and sordid and stupid.” The president “is cutting off civil liberties and using his powers to squelch dissent and enrich himself in such thoroughly illegal ways, it’s kind of mindblowing”, Spiegelman says, and he finds himself watching in alarm as the “plutocrat in chief” and his “few dozen toadies” get ever richer while ordinary Americans struggle and suffer a “new indignity every day”. He has no hesitation in describing the Trump administration as fascist. “It’s fascism,” he says. “It’s not nazism, per se, but it has a template that it’s following. And it does have to do with othering, which is the basis of what Maus is about, it’s: ‘OK, you guys are mice, we’re cats.’” Maus is among the many books to be banned by various Republican school boards in recent years, but Spiegelman says he has a “predilection” for producing the kind of art people will seek to ban. Sales of Maus spiked in response to the bans.

“I tend to be pessimistic, but this is worse than most things I know,” he says of American politics. “I just don’t see how we get out of this.” The media are struggling with how to convey the stakes in this post-truth era, he explains, the courts are packed with Trump appointees, democratic norms have been destroyed, and there is no effective opposition. The Republicans are “at this point the equivalent of made men in the mafia,” Spiegelman says, “they’ve committed a murder, they’re complicit in something and they have to keep moving as a complicit unit, so it’s very hard to get someone to blow the whistle and say ‘This is crazy.’” The US needs a “counter-revolution”, Spiegelman says. “But I don’t know where to look for it because the Democrats are so timid.”

An alert sounds on Spiegelman’s phone, and for a moment he is flustered, trying to figure out why on Earth this thing is producing noise. “In some ways I’m slowing down, in other ways I’m still doing what interests me, and sometimes I’m capable of being interested in something more challenging, sometimes less,” he says. He plans, after this interview, to work on a lithograph, his friend having dropped off some stone for him to carve. He hopes to keep living and working in Soho for the rest of his life – but his apartment is a walk-up, and he concedes fate might have other ideas for him. “Anyone can be a genius at 25; at 50 it takes some doing,” Spiegelman writes in one comic. What about at 78, I ask? “I feel like an idiot at this point!” he jokes. “I can’t think the way I thought when I was 25,” he says. He has become more forgetful, for instance, but takes consolation in knowing he can still produce challenging, original art. “There’s still enough wiring that makes it somewhat unorthodox, but I don’t think I’m as far off the grid as I had been.”

entries.title: Rebecca Perry: ‘Lorca hit me like a bolt of lightning’
entries.summary: The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris LessingMy earliest reading memory Reading On the Ning Nang Nong by Spike Milligan, aged five or so, sitting on the floor of the bedroom I shared with my brother – who, in my memory, was sitting on the carpet next to me.My favourite book growing up I had a collection of fairytales in a big yellow
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

Reading On the Ning Nang Nong by Spike Milligan, aged five or so, sitting on the floor of the bedroom I shared with my brother – who, in my memory, was sitting on the carpet next to me.

My favourite book growing up

I had a collection of fairytales in a big yellow hardback, which I was totally entranced by from around the age of seven to 10. I’ll never forget the feeling of despair on turning the page and discovering that the Little Mermaid had become foam on the surface of the water; it was a very early lesson in the helplessness of the reader in the face of a story’s destiny. In particular, though, I loved a Scottish fairytale called The Black Bull of Norroway, which I think, in many ways, has been under the surface of everything I’ve ever written.

The book that changed me as a teenager

Collected Plays by Federico García Lorca, which I studied for GCSE drama and led me to seek out his poetry. It would be impossible for me to think about my adolescent relationship to reading, and my relationship as an adult to language, without Lorca. I remember these lines from City That Does Not Sleep hitting me like a bolt of lightning: “… and the man who rushes out with his / spirit broken will meet on the street corner / the unbelievable alligator quiet beneath / the tender protest of the stars”.

The writer who changed my mind

Frank O’Hara, which I know is one of the most predictable answers a poet can give, but for good reason. All of the poetry I’d studied up to the point of discovering him felt deeply serious, almost something not to be touched. Then you read O’Hara and it’s like: OK, life!

The book that made me want to be a writer

I really don’t think this is something that happened to me. I have just written for as long as I can remember and, at a certain point as an adult, I realised that normal living people can write books if they want to, if they’re lucky, and that maybe I would like to try to do that. To answer a slightly different question, Percival Everett’s astonishing The Trees was the book that made me feel I might be able to write a novel.

The book I reread

Anne Carson’s Glass and God, in particular The Glass Essay. It’s basically perfect – my go-to text for resetting my brain and being reminded, within the space of a page, about the capacities of writing.

The book I could never read again

JK Rowling’s Harry Potter series was a huge part of my childhood, but it’s art that’s firmly not to be separated from artist, in this case.

The book I discovered later in life

I don’t think I read Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook until I was in my 30s – but really, any time is the perfect time to discover this novel.

The book I am currently reading

A proof of Compensation by Augustine Cerf, which so far is brilliant, and My Garden (Book) by Jamaica Kincaid, which I often pick up and read a page or two of between other things. I’m also rereading Doom Painting by AK Blakemore, out in September. It’s a phenomenal achievement – I don’t know how she did it.

My comfort read

The poetry collection Adam by Gboyega Odubanjo, who died in 2023. I keep this book on the shelf directly above my desk and when the loss of him feels particularly impossible, I take it down, read a poem and remember he’s there on the page.

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry is published by Granta. It won the 2026 Waterstones debut fiction prize and is longlisted for the Booker prize. To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com

entries.content:
The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian (Hutchinson Heinemann, £18.99)

American bestseller Bohjalian deserves to be far better known in the UK, although, as the first line of his 26th novel points out, “It is neither virtue nor might that rules the world; it’s luck”. Mira Winston’s luck began early, as she was born into a rich family, clever enough to secure a place at Yale, and a talented enough golfer to consider turning pro, but things change dramatically in 1978 when, at the age of 18, a ball she hits on a driving range smashes the temporal bone of a young caddy, killing him almost instantly. The freak accident turns out to be rather more complicated than first thought, not least because it becomes karmically conflated, in Mira’s mind, with her relationship with a married man twice her age. Told as a memoir, with Mira looking back on the derailment of her life and chronicling society’s changing perceptions of agency and privilege, this literary thriller is a masterfully executed ace.

Claws Out! by Bella Mackie (Borough, £20)

Mackie’s third novel centres on Diana, a manipulative grifter whose previous three husbands have died, apparently of natural causes. She’s in the process of getting her feet under the fourth mark’s prosperous Hampstead table when she encounters opposition. David Farrand’s “entitled but otherwise entirely average” daughter Catriona isn’t going to give up her father or her inheritance without a fight, and when she starts investigating Diana’s past, she discovers that her former stepchildren are convinced of foul play. Meanwhile, Diana’s own son, a feckless charmer, is also hoping to benefit from his mother’s matrimonial plans. Some readers may find the arch authorial tone grating, and the sharp-eyed will spot at least one major plot development before it occurs, but the incisive social satire, vinegary humour and expert pacing will keep you laughing as you turn the pages.

Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang, translated by Shanna Tan (Doubleday, £14.99)

In a fictional Korean city, green-fingered trauma survivor Yoohee realises her dream of opening a plant shop. Although she remains courteous and self-effacing, her long-held conviction that humans, like plants, repay attention and tenderness, has worn thin, and when an errant boyfriend fails to improve, she repurposes him as fertiliser. She begins offering her overwhelmingly female customer base an additional service, ridding them of abusive men, but a young detective notices that the shop is the only common point of reference in a string of otherwise unconnected disappearances, and a game of cat and mouse ensues. This “weird girl” tale of female revenge is politely told, the mechanics of dismemberment happening off the page, and although the villains tend towards the cartoonish, the atmosphere is such that one can almost inhale the damp, scented air of our heroine’s lush botanical haven as she calmly puts the world to rights.

Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne (Chatto & Windus, £18.99)

Osborne’s books often feature morally ambiguous expats in exotic locations; here it’s American investigator Tyler Sedgewick, in Turkey to track down Chana Knight at the behest of her father. Posing as a writer, Tyler worms his way into the young woman’s friendship group; Chana, Adam, Diana and Marco are the delinquent, sensation-seeking offspring of wealthy parents, who first met at a California reform school for rich kids, and became self-styled radicals. Now, they have walked out of their respective lives with the intention of atoning for their privileged existences through a “meaningfully violent act” against “a prominent American target”. Tyler, who has become dangerously drawn to Chana, does not realise the extent to which he is being used, and soon attracts the attention of the Turkish intelligence agency. There are echoes of both Graham Greene and Patricia Highsmith here, but Osborne’s sense of place and ability create an undercurrent of menace all his own.

Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth (Macmillan, £16.99)

The titular character of Australian Hepworth’s latest is a stroppy, sarcastic 81-year-old, living under a pseudonym in a quiet Melbourne suburb. More than 60 years earlier, Mabel Waller became the youngest person in Australian history to be convicted of murder. Now she keeps herself to herself, but Persephone, the lonely young daughter of a neighbour, is determined to be friends, and slowly Mabel, whose own desolate childhood with her wealthy but uninterested parents is gradually revealed in flashbacks, begins to thaw. But someone has discovered her past and is sending anonymous letters, and when the elderly man next door dies unexpectedly, she becomes the prime suspect. Although crime fiction aficionados may figure out at least one plot twist early on, Mabel’s cantankerous facade, behind which the fuzzy outlines of loss, trauma and misunderstanding gradually sharpen into focus, and the growing warmth of the intergenerational friendship, make this a genuinely moving and surprisingly funny read.
